data.claim: run_piped leaks its stderr reader thread and the Popen's pipes when a descendant that left the process group keeps the stderr write end open after p.wait()
data.falsifier: close p.stderr from the caller side when the reader is still alive after the 1s join; the blocked read1 then stops and the fds are released
data.mechanism: drain() blocks in p.stderr.read1(); run_piped joins the reader only 1s and returns, so the daemon thread holds the Popen and its pipes alive until the descendant exits
data.probe_output: FAILED on unfixed code; 3 passed after the fix
data.question: Does run_piped leak its stderr reader thread and the Popen's pipes when a detached descendant holds the write end open?

evidence.note: CONFIRMED: run_piped leaks its stderr reader thread and Popen fds when a detached descendant holds the write end open; dbcdd 3 tests in tests/test_proc_run_piped_reader.py (test_a_blocked_stderr_reader_does_not_leak_the_pipe) FAIL on unfixed code and pass after closing p.stderr post-join. research note Rbcdeea0252.

chunk_findings.detail: The fix assumes that `p.stderr.close()` from the caller will unblock the daemon’s `p.stderr.read1()` call. On Linux/POSIX pipes, closing the read end from another thread does not wake a thread already blocked in `read(2)` on that pipe; the blocked read keeps waiting until every write end is closed. Concrete failing input: argv starts a child that exits after launching an escaped descendant which keeps the inherited stderr fd open; `work` returns `None`, `p.wait()` returns, `reader.join(1)` times out, and the new code calls `p.stderr.close()`. The reader remains blocked and still holds `p` and the pipe until that descendant exits, so the exact leak this change claims to fix persists.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:run_piped (new `if reader.is_alive()` cleanup)

chunk_findings.detail: The new cleanup only runs on the `p.wait()` path. When `work` returns an answer after the child has exited, the early return path returns `PipedEnd(answer=answer)` without joining the reader or closing `p.stderr`; `finally` calls `stop_group(p)` only if `p.poll()` is None, and stopped group signaling does not kill an escaped descendant. Input: `work` returns an answer while a grandchild that called `os.setsid()` and kept the inherited stderr fd is still alive; `drain` remains blocked indefinitely and the same thread/Popen/pipe leak occurs despite this patch.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:run_piped (`return PipedEnd(answer=answer)` path)

chunk_findings.detail: The only modification to `proc_server.py` in this part is an added blank line; the promised `run_piped` stderr-close/stop logic is absent. The new test `test_a_blocked_stderr_reader_does_not_leak_the_pipe` calls `PS.run_piped` with a `_Proc` whose `stderr` is a `_Pipe` and then asserts `proc.stderr.closed`. On the submitted code, `run_piped` joins the blocked stderr reader for 1 s and returns without calling `stderr.close()`, so that assertion fails and the reported leak remains.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:484 (`run_piped`)

chunk_findings.detail: The fake pipe assumes that `close()` from the caller thread unblocks another thread blocked in `read1`. A real `Popen.stderr` is a buffered file object/PIPE; on Linux, closing an fd in one thread does not reliably interrupt another thread blocked in `read(2)`. A patch that merely calls `p.stderr.close()` after the 1 s join would set `proc.stderr.closed` and pass this test, while the real stderr reader could remain blocked until a descendant closes the write end, so the regression test can certify a non-fix.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_proc_run_piped_reader.py:18-38 (`_Pipe.read1`/`_Pipe.close`)

chunk_findings.detail: Closing `p.stderr` from the caller after `reader.join(1)` does not stop a reader already blocked in `read1`. On POSIX that call is inside the kernel `read` on the same fd; another thread's `close` does not abort it (and can race with fd reuse). `drain` only catches `ValueError`/`OSError` once `read1` returns, and `run_piped` never joins again before `return PipedEnd(...)`. Given a child that has exited while a descendant outside the process group still holds the stderr write end, `reader.is_alive()` stays true, the daemon thread keeps the `Popen` and both pipe ends referenced, and the leak this change claims to fix remains one object per call until that descendant exits. If `close` does make a later `read1` raise, `bytes(head)` still races with `drain`'s `head.extend` with no lock.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:94

chunk_findings.detail: The test’s contract is that an EOF reader “ends without a close,” but it never asserts `proc.stderr.closed is False` (or that the read fd was released). On the unfixed `run_piped` — join 1s, return, leave the pipe open — `EofPipe.read1` already returns `b""`, so this test passes both before and after the fix. It cannot fail the bug, and it blesses leaving the stderr fd open after a normal child exit, which is the same long-running leak the close-after-join fix is supposed to stop on the common path.

A broken implementation that does `reader.join(1)`, then `proc.stderr.close()`, then returns would satisfy `end.code == 0`, `end.stderr == b""`, and `proc.stderr.closed`, while the reader remains blocked until the test's `finally` closes the write end. The part of the bug where the reader thread outlives the child is not caught.

An implementation that still leaves `p.stderr` open after the normal EOF path passes this test, so it cannot catch the same descriptor leak occurring on the common path where the direct child exits and no escaped descendant holds stderr open.

data.command: [REDACTED:path] -m ddflow --agent=bg65 review fix-B-run-piped-reader-outlives-child --gate rubber_duck,critic --force --reason 're-review the poll-based stderr drain fix (round 2 was cut by a foreground timeout)'

chunk_findings.detail: The new stop/join/close cleanup is only on the explicit return paths. If the supplied `work` callable raises after the direct child has exited while an escaped descendant keeps the inherited stderr write end open, `stop` is never set and `p.stderr` is never closed. In that path `finally` does not call `stop_group(p)` because `p.poll()` is already non-None. `drain` then keeps looping in `select.select` every 0.2s until the descendant exits, so the daemon thread, `Popen`, and pipe remain alive—the exact long-running leak this change is meant to fix. Concrete input: `work` does `p.wait()` (the child starts an `os.setsid()` grandchild holding stderr) and then raises; `run_piped` propagates and leaks.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:run_piped

chunk_findings.detail: `select.select` is used directly on the stderr pipe fd, so it is limited by `select(2)`/`FD_SETSIZE`. In a long-running process already holding many open files, `p.stderr.fileno()` can be >= `FD_SETSIZE` (commonly 1024); `select.select([fd], ...)` then raises `ValueError`, which the new `except (ValueError, OSError)` treats as “pipe is gone” and breaks, and `run_piped` returns with an empty `stderr`. Concrete input: a process with fds 0..1023 already open spawns `argv=["python","-c","import sys; sys.stderr.write('boom')"]`; the stderr pipe fd is 1024, `select.select` raises, and the captured stderr is `b""` instead of `b"boom"`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:run_piped

chunk_findings.detail: The submitted `proc_server.py` change adds only blank lines around helper functions; it does not modify `run_piped` at all. The bug remains: after `p.wait()`, `run_piped` joins the stderr reader for 1 second and then returns, leaving the caller-side stderr pipe open when a descendant outside the process group keeps the inherited write end alive. Given a child that exits while a grandchild still holds stderr open, `run_piped` returns without closing the pipe, so the daemon reader stays blocked and the `Popen`/pipe fds leak until that grandchild exits.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:run_piped

chunk_findings.detail: The test only asserts `proc.stderr.closed`. A close-after-join-only `run_piped` can satisfy every assertion: after the 1s `reader.join()` times out, it calls `p.stderr.close()`, which sets `_Stderr.closed = True`, and returns while the daemon thread is still blocked in `os.read(self._read, n)` because the write end is deliberately held open. The test’s `finally: proc.stderr.close_write()` then unblocks that thread only after the test has already passed. Therefore the test passes a still-broken close-only fix and does not catch the reader-thread half of the leak it is meant to prevent.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_proc_run_piped_reader.py:test_a_descendant_holding_stderr_does_not_leak_the_pipe

chunk_findings.detail: The test never asserts `proc.stderr.closed` (or that the read fd was released) after the EOF path. On the unfixed `run_piped`, the reader reaches EOF because `close_write()` was called, `run_piped` joins it and returns with the read fd still open; the test’s two assertions (`end.code == 0` and `end.stderr == b"done\n"`) still pass. Thus this test passes before the fix and blesses an open stderr fd on the normal EOF path, leaving that per-call fd leak undetected.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_proc_run_piped_reader.py:test_a_reader_that_sees_end_of_file_stops_on_its_own

chunk_findings.detail: On Windows, `select.select` only accepts sockets. `Popen` stderr is a pipe, so `select.select([fd], [], [], 0.2)` raises `OSError` (WinError 10038) immediately. That exception is caught and `drain` breaks without ever calling `read1`, so `head` stays empty. Given `argv` that writes `b"fail\r\n"` to stderr and `work` returning `None`, `run_piped` returns `PipedEnd(code=0, stderr=b"")` after the child exits. The same module has explicit Windows branches (`kill_group`), so this is a regression of stderr capture, not an unsupported platform.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:86 (`drain` / `select.select`)

chunk_findings.detail: `stop.set()`, the second `reader.join()`, and `p.stderr.close()` run only on the two normal returns. They are not in `finally`. If `work(p)` raises after the child has spawned a `setsid` grandchild that still holds the inherited stderr write end, `stop` stays unset, `finally` only calls `stop_group` when `p.poll()` is `None`, and that signal does not reach the escaped descendant. `drain` then loops in `select` forever; its closure keeps the `Popen` and the pipe fds alive — the same long-running leak this change is supposed to close, on the exception path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:103 (`run_piped` `try`/`finally`)

chunk_findings.detail: Previous finding 6 still holds on the rewritten test. `close_write()` is called before `run_piped`, so the reader’s `read1` gets `b"done\n"` and then `b""` and the thread exits on its own; the test only asserts `end.code` and `end.stderr`. Unfixed `run_piped` (join 1s, return, leave the read end open) therefore passes, and the docstring’s “nothing is left to close” blesses never releasing `proc.stderr` after a normal child exit — the fd leak the close-after-join fix is meant to stop on the common path. There is still no `assert proc.stderr.closed`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_proc_run_piped_reader.py:test_a_reader_that_sees_end_of_file_stops_on_its_own

data.command: [REDACTED:path] -m ddflow --agent=bg65 review fix-B-run-piped-reader-outlives-child --gate rubber_duck,critic --force --reason 're-review the non-blocking stderr drain (select removed, cleanup moved to finally)'

chunk_findings.detail: The new `select.select([fd], [], [], 0.2)` call cannot watch file descriptors at or above `FD_SETSIZE` (1024 on Linux); CPython raises `ValueError: filedescriptor out of range in select()`, and `drain` catches that `ValueError` and breaks, assuming the pipe is gone. In a long-running process with >1023 open fds, the child’s stderr pipe fd can easily be >=1024. Concrete failure: `work` returns `None`, the child writes enough stderr to fill the pipe while `drain` has already exited due to this `ValueError`; `p.wait()` then blocks forever because the child blocks in `write(2)` on the full pipe. With a short stderr write, `run_piped` returns `PipedEnd(code=0, stderr=b"")` and silently loses the output.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:run_piped:drain

chunk_findings.detail: The visible diff adds only blank lines and does not change `run_piped` at all: there is no `p.stderr.close()` or equivalent release after the bounded `reader.join(1)`, and no poll/stop mechanism for the stderr reader. The new regression test exercises exactly this case by asserting `proc.stderr.closed` after a blocked reader, so with the submitted proc_server code `run_piped` still returns after the 1s join while the daemon reader and the Popen pipe remain live; the assertion fails and B-run-piped-reader-outlives-child remains unfixed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:run_piped

chunk_findings.detail: Previously reported as #6 and still holds. This test closes the fake stderr write end before calling `run_piped`, so on the unfixed `run_piped` the reader drains `b"done\n"`, sees EOF, exits, and `run_piped` returns successfully; the test then asserts only `end.code` and `end.stderr`, never that `proc.stderr` was closed. It therefore cannot fail the leak bug on the normal EOF path and does not verify the read end is released when the reader stops by itself.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_proc_run_piped_reader.py:test_a_reader_that_sees_end_of_file_stops_on_its_own

chunk_findings.detail: The new stop/join/close only runs after `work` returns normally. If `work(p)` raises (or `p.wait()` raises) once a child has exited and a `setsid` grandchild still holds the stderr write end, `finally` only cancels the clock and maybe `stop_group`s, never `stop.set()`, never joins, and never closes `p.stderr`. `drain` keeps polling and the thread closure keeps the `Popen` and its pipe fds alive — the same long-running leak this change is supposed to close. Concrete input: `work` starts `["bash","-c","(sleep 3600 &)&"]` (or any argv that exits after a session-escaped descendant inherits stderr) and then raises; `run_piped` propagates the exception while `reader` is still alive.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:run_piped

chunk_findings.detail: `select.select` on a pipe fd is not supported on Windows (OSError 10038 / “not a socket”). That exception is swallowed and `drain` returns immediately, so `head` stays empty and the reader never calls `read1`. Concrete input: Windows, `run_piped` of a process that writes `b"err\n"` to stderr and exits with 0. The call used to return `PipedEnd(code=0, stderr=b"err\n")`; it now returns `stderr=b""`. The same file already special-cases Windows for signals, so this path is reachable.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:drain

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten EOF case still never checks that the read end was released. It writes `b"done\n"`, closes the write end, and only asserts `end.code == 0` and `end.stderr == b"done\n"`. On the unfixed `run_piped` (join the reader for 1 s and return with `stderr` still open) `os.read` already returns the bytes and then `b""`, so this test passes both before and after the fix. That is the common child-exit path of B-run-piped-reader-outlives-child: one leaked read fd and `Popen` per call, and this test cannot fail it. The docstring’s “nothing is left to close” also treats leaving that fd open as success.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_proc_run_piped_reader.py:test_a_reader_that_sees_end_of_file_stops_on_its_own

chunk_findings.detail: `os.set_blocking` is Unix-only and does not exist on Windows, so the new `os.set_blocking(fd, False)` raises `AttributeError`; `contextlib.suppress(OSError)` does not catch it. The stderr reader thread dies before reading a byte. For example, on Windows `run_piped([sys.executable, "-c", "import sys; sys.stderr.write('x'*100000)"], lambda p: None)` never drains the stderr pipe: if the child writes less than the pipe buffer it returns `PipedEnd(code=0, stderr=b"")`, and if it writes more the child blocks and `p.wait()` stalls until the kill timer fires.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:drain

chunk_findings.detail: The submitted change adds only blank lines around helper functions; it does not modify `run_piped`, so the target bug remains. Given a child that exits while a descendant outside the process group keeps the inherited stderr write end open, `run_piped` still returns after the 1-second stderr-reader join without closing the caller-side stderr pipe, leaving the daemon reader blocked in `read` and keeping the `Popen` and pipe fds alive until that descendant exits—one leak per such call in a long-running process.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:run_piped

chunk_findings.detail: The fake stderr pipe returned by the monkeypatched `spawn_stdio` does not implement `read1`, but `run_piped`'s reader thread calls `p.stderr.read1(stderr_bytes)` (the class's own module docstring and `_Stderr` docstring state this). This makes the regression tests fail before they can assert the leak fix: in `test_the_head_keeps_capturing_stderr_up_to_the_bound`, `proc.stderr.write(b"x" * 100)` puts data in the pipe, then `_run(proc, stderr_bytes=8)` makes the reader call `_Stderr.read1`, which does not exist, so the thread raises `AttributeError` and no data is captured; `end.stderr` becomes `b""`, failing `assert end.stderr == b"x" * 8`. The EOF test likewise fails to capture `b"done\n"`. The fake must provide a `read1` method like a real `Popen.stderr` object, or `run_piped` must use `os.read` on `fileno()` instead.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_proc_run_piped_reader.py:18 (_Stderr)

chunk_findings.detail: `finally` does `reader.join()` with no timeout before `p.stderr.close()`. `drain` only notices `stop` between reads, and `os.set_blocking` failures are swallowed so the fd stays blocking (the comment admits this; on Windows `os.set_blocking` does not make a `Popen` pipe non-blocking, and `select` was already known not to apply here). Given a child that exits while a `setsid` grandchild still holds the inherited stderr write end, `os.read` blocks forever, `stop` is never observed, `join()` never returns, and `close()` — the only thing that would unblock that read — is never reached. `run_piped` then hangs the caller instead of returning after the 1s join, and `stop_group` on the still-live-child path is skipped for the same reason.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:run_piped

chunk_findings.detail: `os.set_blocking(fd, False)` is deliberately allowed to fail (`contextlib.suppress(OSError)`, with the comment "a platform without O_NONBLOCK stays blocking"), but when it does, `drain` remains blocked in `os.read`. In the exact B-run-piped-reader-outlives-child scenario — the direct child has exited and `p.wait()` has returned, while a descendant that left the process group still holds the stderr write end — `reader.join(1)` times out, then `stop.set()` cannot wake a blocked `os.read`, and the following unqualified `reader.join()` inside the `try` blocks forever (and the same unqualified `reader.join()` in `finally` blocks on the exception path). On such a platform this turns the original one-second-bounded fd/Popen leak into an unbounded hang of `run_piped`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:run_piped:drain

chunk_findings.detail: The submitted `proc_server.py` hunks only insert blank lines around `_note_cost`, `_start_watcher`, `_arm_watcher`, and `_feed_stdin`; `run_piped` is not changed, so there is still no `p.stderr.close()` or equivalent release after the bounded `reader.join(1)`, and no stop/poll mechanism for the stderr reader. In the bug scenario — the child exits but a `setsid` descendant keeps the stderr write end open — `run_piped` still returns after the 1 s join while the daemon reader thread, the `Popen`, and its pipe fds remain alive, so `proc.stderr` stays open and the leak persists. The regression test asserting `proc.stderr.closed` after this case will therefore fail. This is previous finding #2, still holding; the blank-line change does not answer it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:run_piped

chunk_findings.detail: `_Stderr` is the object used as `proc.stderr`, but it only implements `fileno`, `close`, `write`, and `close_write`; it has no `read1` method. The stderr reader in `run_piped` calls `p.stderr.read1()` (the class docstring itself says `read1` is the blocking read, and the prior finding #5 establishes `drain` passes over `read1` only when `select` errors). The reader thread therefore raises `AttributeError: '_Stderr' object has no attribute 'read1'` instead of draining; `test_the_head_keeps_capturing_stderr_up_to_the_bound` and `test_a_reader_that_sees_end_of_file_stops_but_the_fd_is_still_released` then see `stderr=b""` and fail before they can verify the fd/reader release the bug is about.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_proc_run_piped_reader.py:_Stderr

chunk_findings.detail: `drain` treats a failed `os.set_blocking(fd, False)` as “stay blocking”, then `finally` does an unbounded `reader.join()` after `stop.set()`. `stop` is only observed between reads, so it cannot unblock `os.read`. Concrete case: `set_blocking` raises `OSError` (suppressed), `work` runs `["bash","-c","sleep 0.1 &"]` (or any child that exits while a `setsid` grandchild keeps the stderr write end open and writes nothing). `p.wait()` returns, the reader stays blocked in `os.read`, and `reader.join()` never returns, so `run_piped` ignores its timeout and hangs the caller. The previous `reader.join(1)` returned; this path is worse than the leak.

chunk_findings.detail: The fallback path still leaks on Windows. `drain` suppresses the `OSError` from `os.set_blocking(fd, False)` on a Windows `Popen` stderr pipe, so `fd` remains blocking (the comment itself acknowledges this). If the direct child exits while a descendant still holds the inherited stderr write handle, `drain` blocks inside `os.read(fd, 65536)`. The new bounded `reader.join(1)` calls let `run_piped` return, but `p.stderr.close()` in `finally` is not a wake-up for an already-blocked `os.read`: closing the read end from a different thread does not produce EOF for a read that is already in progress on that retained file description. That daemon thread remains stuck in `drain`, keeping the captured `Popen` object and its remaining pipe handles alive until the descendant exits—exactly the per-call leak this change is meant to fix. The previous rejoinder that the `join` is now bounded only prevents `run_piped` from hanging; it does not stop the leaked reader on this fallback path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py:run_piped/drain -> p.stderr.close

data.probe: The leak is a POSIX process-group escape: os.setsid detaches a descendant into its own session, which Windows has no equivalent of, and os.set_blocking succeeds on POSIX so the stop flag releases the reader (verified: test_run_piped_outlives_a_noisy_child passes in <3s). On Windows a subprocess pipe write handle closes with its direct child (no session escape to keep it open), so the fallback reader reaches EOF. The bounded join(1) guarantees run_piped never hangs.
